paragraphs: It is not a new observation that a people who are intelligent and well-informed, as the Americans are, seldom adopt a mistaken opinion about their interests and hold to it steadily for many years. That consideration naturally creates great respect for the view that the people of America have long and uniformly held: that it matters greatly for them to stay firmly united under one federal government, given enough power for all general and national purposes.
The more closely I examine the reasons that seem to have given rise to this opinion, the more convinced I am that they are compelling and conclusive.

A wise and free people must give their attention to many things, and providing for their SAFETY seems to come first. The SAFETY of the people doubtless depends on a great variety of circumstances and considerations, and so leaves wide room for anyone who wishes to define it precisely and comprehensively.

For now I mean to consider it only as it concerns the preservation of peace and tranquillity. This includes security against dangers from FOREIGN ARMS AND INFLUENCE and against dangers of the LIKE KIND that arise from domestic causes. The former comes first in order, so it is proper to discuss it first. Let us therefore examine whether the people are right in thinking that a cordial Union, under an effective national government, gives them the best security that can be devised against HOSTILITIES from abroad.

The number of wars that have happened, or will happen, in the world will always be found proportionate to the number and weight of the causes, whether REAL or PRETENDED, that PROVOKE or INVITE them. If this remark is just, it is useful to ask whether UNITED AMERICA is likely to give as many JUST causes of war as DISUNITED America would. If it turns out that United America will probably give the fewest, it follows that in this respect the Union does the most to keep the people at peace with other nations.

The JUST causes of war come, for the most part, from one of two sources: violation of treaties or direct violence. America has already made treaties with no fewer than six foreign nations, and all of them except Prussia are maritime powers, and so able to annoy and injure us. She also carries on extensive commerce with Portugal, Spain, and Britain, and with the last two she must also reckon with the fact that they are her neighbors.

It is of high importance to the peace of America that she observe the laws of nations toward all these powers. To me it is evident that one national government would do this more perfectly and punctually than thirteen separate States, or three or four distinct confederacies, could.

First, once an effective national government is established, the best men in the country will not only be willing to serve but will generally be the ones chosen to run it. Town or country influence, or some other narrow influence, may put men into State assemblies, senates, courts of justice, or executive departments. But offices under the national government will require a wider and more extensive reputation for talents and other qualifications. This is especially so because the national government will have the widest field to choose from and will never suffer the shortage of suitable persons that is not uncommon in some of the States. It will follow that the administration, the political counsels, and the judicial decisions of the national government will be wiser, more systematic, and more judicious than those of the individual States. They will therefore be more satisfactory to other nations, and more SAFE for us.

Second, under the national government, treaties and parts of treaties, like the laws of nations, will always be interpreted in one sense and carried out in the same way. But rulings on the same points and questions will not always agree or be consistent across thirteen States, or three or four confederacies. This will be so because of the variety of independent courts and judges appointed by different and independent governments, and also because of the differing local laws and interests that may affect and influence them. The wisdom of the convention in placing such questions under the jurisdiction and judgment of courts appointed by, and answerable only to, one national government cannot be praised too highly.

Third, the prospect of present loss or gain may often tempt the governing party in one or two States to depart from good faith and justice. But those temptations do not reach the other States and so have little or no influence on the national government. The temptation will therefore be fruitless, and good faith and justice will be preserved. The case of the treaty of peace with Britain adds great weight to this reasoning.

Fourth, even if the governing party in a State were disposed to resist such temptations, they may, and commonly do, result from circumstances peculiar to the State, and may affect a great number of its inhabitants. The governing party may then be unable, even if willing, to prevent the injustice that is planned or to punish those who commit it. But the national government is not affected by those local circumstances. It will not be led to commit the wrong itself, and it will not lack the power or the will to prevent or punish the wrong when others commit it.

So far, therefore, as violations of treaties and of the laws of nations, whether intended or accidental, give JUST causes of war, they are less to be feared under one general government than under several lesser ones. In that respect the former does the most to favor the SAFETY of the people.

Now consider those just causes of war that come from direct and unlawful violence. It seems to me equally clear that one good national government gives far more security against dangers of that sort than can be had from any other source.

The reason is that such violence is more often caused by the passions and interests of a part than of the whole: of one or two States rather than of the Union. Not one Indian war has yet been caused by aggressions of the present federal government, feeble as it is. But there are several instances of Indian hostilities provoked by the improper conduct of individual States, which were unable or unwilling to restrain or punish offenses and so gave occasion for the slaughter of many innocent inhabitants.

Spanish and British territories border on some States and not on others, and this naturally confines the causes of quarrel mainly to the States along the border. If any States are to provoke war with these nations by direct violence, they will be the bordering ones, acting on sudden irritation and a quick sense of apparent interest or injury. Nothing can prevent that danger so effectively as a national government, whose wisdom and prudence will not be clouded by the passions of the parties directly concerned.

But the national government will not only give fewer just causes of war. It will also be better placed to settle them peacefully. It will be more temperate and cool, and in that respect, as in others, better able to act with deliberation than the offending State. The pride of states, like the pride of men, naturally leads them to justify everything they do, and it stands in the way of their admitting, correcting, or repairing their errors and offenses. The national government will not be affected by this pride in such cases. It will proceed with moderation and fairness to consider and decide on the best means of freeing them from the difficulties that threaten them.

Besides, it is well known that a strong united nation can often offer acknowledgments, explanations, and compensation that are accepted as satisfactory, when the very same offers would be rejected as unsatisfactory coming from a State or confederacy of little consideration or power.

In 1685 the state of Genoa, having offended Louis XIV, tried to appease him. He demanded that they send their Doge, or chief executive, accompanied by four of their senators, to FRANCE, to ask his pardon and receive his terms. For the sake of peace they had to submit. Would he ever have demanded or accepted the same humiliation from Spain, or Britain, or any other POWERFUL nation?
